    Bot protection (ALTCHA)#

    Before a form is sent, the browser solves a moderately heavy computation, and the server checks the answer (proof-of-work). Unlike CAPTCHAs that make people read distorted text, the user ticks "I'm not a robot" and waits a few seconds.

    • No outside service to sign up for. Unlike reCAPTCHA or Turnstile, neither you nor your tenants register anywhere
    • No separate server. Creating and checking challenges both happen inside the app
    • No domains to register. Tenants on their own domains work as they are, however many there are
    • Your users' data does not leave your app

    The browser side is the ALTCHA widget (altcha 3.x, MIT). jimble provides the two server pieces: a route that hands out challenges, and a filter that checks answers.

    What you write#

    get("/altcha/challenge", Altcha::challenge);

path("/contact", () -> {
	before(Altcha::verify);
	get("", context -> context.response().text("form"));
	post("", context -> context.response().text("ok"));
});

    Altcha::verify works like before: it applies only to the block you write it in. Methods that do not change state (GET and so on) pass straight through, so it can share a block with the route that shows the form.

    Put the key in the configuration. At least 32 characters, and always read it from the environment.

    altcha {
	secret = ${?ALTCHA_SECRET}
}

    With no key, or a short one, both handing out a challenge (/altcha/challenge) and checking an answer stop with an error.

    Placing the widget#

    <script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/altcha@3.5.0/dist/main/altcha.js"></script>

<form method="post" action="/contact">
	...
	<altcha-widget challenge="/altcha/challenge"></altcha-widget>
	<button>Send</button>
</form>
    • Pin the version (not a range like altcha@3). Installing it from npm and serving it yourself is fine too
    • The widget puts the solved answer in the form's altcha field
    • If you send with fetch instead of a form, put the answer in the JSON body's altcha or in the X-Altcha header
    • If your app sets a CSP, the widget uses Web Workers; check ALTCHA's documentation and add what it needs (jimble sends no CSP by default)

    When it refuses#

    No answer, a malformed one, an expired one, a tampered one, or one already used: all of these are 403. The messages come out of jimble in Japanese; the English in parentheses is a gloss.

    Result (AltchaResult) Message
    MISSING 「ロボットでないことの確認（ALTCHA）が送られていません」（"no ALTCHA answer was sent"）
    MALFORMED 「ロボットでないことの確認（ALTCHA）の形が正しくありません」（"the ALTCHA answer is malformed"）
    EXPIRED 「ロボットでないことの確認（ALTCHA）の期限が切れています。もう一度確かめてください」（"expired; try again"）
    INVALID 「ロボットでないことを確かめられませんでした」（"could not confirm you are not a robot"）
    REPLAYED 「ロボットでないことの確認（ALTCHA）はもう使われています。もう一度確かめてください」（"already used; try again"）

    To show the form again instead of a 403, take the result from Altcha.check.

    post("/contact", context -> {
	AltchaResult result = Altcha.check(context.request().bodyForm().getStringOptional(Altcha.FIELD_NAME));
	if (!result.verified()) {
		// show result.message() and return the form
	}
	...
});

    Careful

    Altcha.check records a passing answer as used. Call it twice with the same answer and the second call returns REPLAYED. Do not call check again inside a route already covered by before(Altcha::verify).

    Each answer passes once#

    Once an answer passes, a "used" mark is kept until the challenge expires, and the same answer is refused after that. The mark lives in the same store as rate limiting (rate_limit.store).

    Careful

    If you run more than one instance, set rate_limit.store to redis or db. With memory, the mark exists only on one instance, so the same answer sent to another instance passes.

    If the store is unavailable (Redis is down, say), the answer passes and the failure is logged. That matches rate limiting: a store outage should not stop every form in the app. The signature and the answer have already been checked.

    Weight and expiry#

    altcha {
	cost        = 5000    # weight of one attempt (PBKDF2 iterations)
	counter_max = 10000   # upper bound of the answer, picked from counter_max / 2 up to counter_max
	expires     = 10m     # how long a challenge stays valid
}

    The browser tries answers from 0 upward, so the work is about cost × answer computations. With the defaults, Chrome on a 10-core Mac took 3.1 seconds for an answer near the upper bound. Older phones take several times that. Heavier settings bother bots more, and people too.

    The widget fetches a challenge when the user touches it, not when the page opens, so the expiry does not need to be long.

    This alone does not stop everything#

    Proof-of-work makes bots spend effort. A bot willing to compute gets through.

    • Limit how often forms are sent with rate limiting (putting it on /altcha/challenge as well limits floods of challenge requests)
    • Limit login attempts with Lockout.attempt (authentication)
